draft.title: Oral history as evidence
card: Oral history is a recorded interview with a person who lived through an event. It is made for the historical record, often years after the event.
It can give personal detail that official records leave out, such as feelings, daily routines and how ordinary people were affected.
Memories can fade, change or be shaped by what the person learned later. An interview can also be shaped by the questions the interviewer asks.
Historians do not throw oral history out. They check its claims against other sources, such as letters, photographs and records made at the time.
draft.remember: Oral history adds personal detail, but it is checked against other sources.

a.q: Why do historians check an oral history interview against other sources?
opts: Memories can fade or change over the years
Interviews never contain any useful detail
Spoken accounts are less honest than written ones
Official records are always more accurate
a.why: Memory can change over time, so claims need support from other evidence. The idea that interviews are useless is wrong: they give personal detail that other sources often lack.
a.clue: Think about what happens to memories as years pass.

b.q: In 2019, Dot is interviewed about the 1974 cyclone that hit Darwin. She describes the night in vivid detail. What is the best way to use her interview?
opts: Use her detail, and check her dates against records
Reject it, because it was recorded long after 1974
Accept every detail, because she was there
Use it only if she remembers the exact date
b.why: Dot's interview offers personal detail, and her dates and facts can be checked against records made at the time. Rejecting it because of the gap in time is too harsh, as oral history is still useful evidence.
b.clue: Useful evidence can still need checking.

a.best: Memories can fade or change over the years

b.best: Use her detail, and check her dates against records

proposal.title: Oral history as evidence
card: Oral history is a recorded interview with a person who lived through an event. It is made for the historical record, often years after the event.

proposal.remember: Oral history adds personal detail, but it is checked against other sources.

a.q: Why do historians check an oral history interview against other sources?
opts: Memories can fade or change as the years pass
Speakers tend to be less honest than letter writers
Interviews give too little personal detail to use
Official records hold more of people's feelings
a.why: Memory can change over time, so an interview's claims need support from other evidence. The problem is not that speakers are less honest: a person can be fully honest and still remember things wrongly.
a.clue: Oral history adds detail. So where could errors creep in?

b.q: In 2019, Dot is interviewed about the 1974 cyclone that hit Darwin. She describes the night in vivid detail. What is the best way to use her interview?
opts: Use her detail, and check her dates against records
Reject it, because it was recorded long after 1974
Accept her account, because she was there
Trust her dates, because vivid memories are accurate
b.why: Dot's interview offers personal detail, and her dates and facts can be checked against records made at the time. Trusting her dates because the memory is vivid is a mistake, as even clear memories can fade or change over 45 years.
b.clue: Useful evidence can still need checking.
